Understanding keloids: when a scar continues to grow beyond healing.

Keloids are a form of abnormal scar formation caused by excessive collagen production, leading to a raised scar that extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound.

They may develop following:
🔹 Acne
🔹 Ear piercings
🔹 Surgical procedures
🔹 Minor cuts or skin injuries

👀 Clinical features of keloids include:
• Raised, thickened scar tissue
• Extension beyond the initial injury site
• Itching, tenderness, or discomfort
• Progressive increase in size over time

⚠️ Unlike typical scars, keloids do not resolve spontaneously and may continue to enlarge if left untreated.

🧬 Risk factors:
• Genetic predisposition
• Darker skin phototypes
• Personal or family history of keloids

Keloids are non-contagious, but often persistent and prone to recurrence, requiring structured medical management.

🛡️ Evidence-based treatment options:
✔️ Intralesional corticosteroid injections
✔️ Silicone-based scar therapy
✔️ Laser-assisted treatments
✔️ Combination protocols for improved control and reduced recurrence

✨ Early intervention is key to achieving better outcomes and minimising progression.

🌍 World TB Day — TB Is Not Just in the Lungs

On World TB Day, it’s important to remember that tuberculosis can also affect the skin. Cutaneous Tuberculosis is a form of extrapulmonary TB that appears on the skin and is often misdiagnosed as fungal infection, chronic wounds, or non-healing skin lesions.

Common signs of skin TB may include:
• Persistent plaques or nodules
• Non-healing ulcers or discharging sinuses
• Warty or crusted lesions
• Slow-growing lesions over months to years

In India, cutaneous TB is treated under the National TB Elimination Programme as extrapulmonary TB with daily anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) using fixed-dose combinations. The standard regimen is 2 months HRZE + 4 months HRE, and early treatment leads to complete cure in most cases.

At SkinSpace Clinic, Goregaon West, Mumbai, dermatologists Dr. Abhay Talathi and Dr. Prajakta Talathi focus on early diagnosis of chronic, non-healing skin lesions through biopsy and timely referral for treatment.

🌍 World Rare Disease Day | Albinism Awareness

Albinism is a rare genetic condition affecting about 1 in 17,000–20,000 people worldwide. It occurs due to reduced or absent melanin, the pigment responsible for skin, hair, and eye color and the body’s natural protection against ultraviolet (UV) radiation.

Because melanin levels are low, individuals with albinism are more vulnerable to:

☀️ Rapid sunburn
☀️ Photosensitivity
☀️ Early sun damage
☀️ Increased long-term UV-related skin risks

Albinism is not contagious. It is usually inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, meaning both parents may be silent carriers. Lifelong sun protection and regular dermatology check-ups are essential to maintain healthy skin.

🛡️ Essential Skin Protection
• Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF 50+)
• Protective clothing and sun barriers
• Regular dermatologic skin examinations
• Early sun-safety education from childhood
